explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Moses says, “…do not be afraid of them; for the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, is with you.” (Deuteronomy 20:1) Horses, chariots and a bigger army, and the instruction is still don't be afraid. The reason is right there in the same verse.

Not quite, friend. Moses says, “…do not be afraid of them; for the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, is with you.” (Deuteronomy 20:1) That's said about horses, chariots and an army larger than Israel's. So the answer is True, and the reason comes in the same breath.

explanations.answer: The LORD their God is with them
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the whole reason. Moses says the LORD their God, who brought them out of Egypt, is with them. Notice he doesn't point at the swords or the numbers. He points at who is standing beside Israel.

explanations.answer: Their swords are stronger than chariots
explanations.explanation: I get why that sounds tempting, but Moses never says a word about swords. He says not to be afraid because the LORD their God, who brought them out of Egypt, is with them. I'd be checking my own sword with sweaty hands, so I'm glad the reason isn't about the sword.

explanations.answer: Their enemies will run away first
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't promise that, friend. He doesn't say what the enemy will do at all. What he says is, “…for the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, is with you.” (Deuteronomy 20:1)

That's the one. Moses says that when they're about to go into battle, the priest is to come forward and address the army. (Deuteronomy 20:2) So the first voice the soldiers hear is the priest's, before the officers speak. A word from the priest right before the fighting begins, that's a good order of things.
A king isn't who Moses names here, friend. He says the priest is to come forward and address the army. (Deuteronomy 20:2) Nobody in these verses is giving a royal speech.
Close, but Moses names someone else. The text says the priest is to come forward and address the army. (Deuteronomy 20:2) The prophet doesn't show up in this part of the passage.

The priest says the opposite, friend. His words are, “Do not be fainthearted or afraid; do not be alarmed or terrified because of them.” That's four different ways of saying don't be afraid. Nobody is told to just keep marching with shaky knees.

That's right, it's False. The priest says, “Do not be fainthearted or afraid; do not be alarmed or terrified because of them.” (Deuteronomy 20:3) Afraid, alarmed, terrified, fainthearted. He stacks them up like he really means it.

Yes, fight. The priest says, “For the LORD your God goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.” (Deuteronomy 20:4) The LORD doesn't just show up to watch. He goes with them to fight for them.

Speaking is the priest's job in this scene, not the part he says the LORD does. His words are, “For the LORD your God goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.” (Deuteronomy 20:4) So the blank is fight.

Waiting is a thing I know plenty about, but it's not in this verse. The priest says the LORD your God goes with them “to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.” (Deuteronomy 20:4) So the word is fight.

Right. The officers ask, “Has any man built a new house and not dedicated it? Let him return home…” (Deuteronomy 20:5) It's an odd thing for an army to say, but it's right there in the text. A man with a brand new house gets sent home.
The officers go the other direction, friend. They say, “Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man dedicate it.” (Deuteronomy 20:5) Nobody is told to lead a charge here.
Selling never comes up, friend. The officers say about that man, “Let him return home…” (Deuteronomy 20:5) The house is the reason he goes home, not something he sells.

explanations.answer: He may die and another man dedicate it
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the officers give. They say, “Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man dedicate it.” (Deuteronomy 20:5) The house is built, and someone else could end up enjoying the dedication of it. I think that's the kind of thing a person would want to see through himself.

explanations.answer: The army already has too many soldiers
explanations.explanation: The officers never say anything about numbers. The reason they give is, “…he may die in battle and another man dedicate it.” (Deuteronomy 20:5) Remember, Moses already told Israel the army across from them might be larger, so this isn't about having extra soldiers.

explanations.answer: His house needs guarding during the battle
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, but the officers don't say it. They say he should go home, “or he may die in battle and another man dedicate it.” (Deuteronomy 20:5) The worry is about him and the dedication, not a guard post.

Yes, married. The officers say, “Has any man become pledged to a woman and not married her? Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man marry her.” (Deuteronomy 20:7) That's the third man on the list, after the house and the vineyard.
Pledged is already past the meeting stage, friend. The officers say, “Has any man become pledged to a woman and not married her?” (Deuteronomy 20:7) The word you want is married.
Visiting isn't what the officers talk about. They say, “Has any man become pledged to a woman and not married her? Let him return home…” (Deuteronomy 20:7) So the missing word is married.

The officers do the reverse, friend. They say, “Is any man afraid or fainthearted? Let him return home…” (Deuteronomy 20:8) Nobody is told to stay and prove anything. A frightened man gets sent home, no speech about being brave.
That's right, it's False. The officers say, “Is any man afraid or fainthearted? Let him return home…” (Deuteronomy 20:8) There's no proving yourself in these words. They send him home.

explanations.answer: So his brothers' hearts won't melt like his
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The officers say, “…so that the hearts of his brothers will not melt like his own.” (Deuteronomy 20:8) Fear can spread, and the officers want to keep it from reaching the men beside him.

explanations.answer: So he can guard the empty houses back home
explanations.explanation: The officers never mention guarding houses, friend. The reason they give is, “…so that the hearts of his brothers will not melt like his own.” (Deuteronomy 20:8) It's about the men standing next to him.

explanations.answer: So he can pray for the army while it fights
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a nice job, but the text doesn't say it. The officers say he goes home “so that the hearts of his brothers will not melt like his own.” (Deuteronomy 20:8) Their concern is the hearts of the other men.

Yes, commanders. The text says, “When the officers have finished addressing the army, they are to appoint commanders to lead it.” (Deuteronomy 20:9) First the speeches, then somebody gets put in charge.
The priest already had his turn earlier in the passage. Here it says the officers “are to appoint commanders to lead it.” (Deuteronomy 20:9) So the word is commanders.
Judges aren't in this verse, friend. After the officers finish speaking, they “are to appoint commanders to lead it.” (Deuteronomy 20:9) The army needs leaders, and that's who they pick.

That's it. Moses says, “When you approach a city to fight against it, you are to make an offer of peace.” (Deuteronomy 20:10) Peace gets offered before any fighting starts. That's a big thing to put first.
Spies aren't what Moses has in mind here. His instruction is, “When you approach a city to fight against it, you are to make an offer of peace.” (Deuteronomy 20:10) Peace comes first.
No trumpets in this passage, friend. Moses says, “When you approach a city to fight against it, you are to make an offer of peace.” (Deuteronomy 20:10) The first step is an offer of peace.

Yes. The text says, “If they accept your offer of peace and open their gates, all the people there will become forced laborers to serve you.” (Deuteronomy 20:11) So accepting peace is the road that doesn't go through a siege.

The text doesn't say that. It says that if they accept peace and open their gates, “all the people there will become forced laborers to serve you.” (Deuteronomy 20:11) Nothing here puts them in the army.
Moving away isn't what the verse says, friend. It says the people there “will become forced laborers to serve you.” (Deuteronomy 20:11) Leaving the land isn't part of it.

That's right. Moses says, “But if they refuse to make peace with you and wage war against you, lay siege to that city.” (Deuteronomy 20:12) The peace offer comes first, and the siege only comes if the city refuses.

It's actually True, friend. Moses says, “But if they refuse to make peace with you and wage war against you, lay siege to that city.” (Deuteronomy 20:12) A city that refuses peace and wages war gets a siege.

That's right. After describing the peace offer, Moses says, “This is how you are to treat all the cities that are far away from you and do not belong to the nations nearby.” (Deuteronomy 20:15) The peace offer is for the far-away cities. The nations nearby are a different case.

It's actually True, friend. Moses says, “This is how you are to treat all the cities that are far away from you and do not belong to the nations nearby.” (Deuteronomy 20:15) That's the offer of peace and everything that follows it. The cities of the nearby nations get a different command.

explanations.answer: So they can't teach Israel what they do for their gods
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Moses gives. He says it's “so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods, and so cause you to sin against the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 20:18) The concern is Israel being led into sin against the LORD. It's a heavy passage, and the text itself gives the reason.

explanations.answer: So Israel can take all of their silver and gold
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't give that reason, friend. He says it's “so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods, and so cause you to sin against the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 20:18) Silver and gold aren't mentioned here.

explanations.answer: So they can't attack Israel's cities from behind
explanations.explanation: That isn't the reason in the text. Moses says it's “so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods, and so cause you to sin against the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 20:18) The worry is about what they'd teach Israel.

Moses says the opposite, friend. “…you must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them, because you can eat their fruit. You must not cut them down.” (Deuteronomy 20:19) Even in a long siege, the fruit trees stay standing.

That's right, it's False. Moses says, “…you must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them, because you can eat their fruit. You must not cut them down.” (Deuteronomy 20:19) He says it twice, so he means it.

Yes, eat. Moses says, “…you must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them, because you can eat their fruit.” (Deuteronomy 20:19) A tree that feeds you is worth more standing than chopped down. That's one reason I'd never chop down a tree that grows cookie dough, if I could find one.
Selling isn't mentioned, friend. Moses says, “…you must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them, because you can eat their fruit.” (Deuteronomy 20:19) The word is eat.
Storing isn't what Moses says. His words are, “…because you can eat their fruit.” (Deuteronomy 20:19) So the blank is eat.

explanations.answer: Building siege works against the city
explanations.explanation: That's right. Moses says, “But you may destroy the trees that you know do not produce fruit. Use them to build siege works against the city that is waging war against you, until it falls.” (Deuteronomy 20:20) The trees with no fruit are the ones Israel may use. The fruit trees are off limits.

Shields aren't mentioned, friend. Moses says Israel may use those trees “to build siege works against the city that is waging war against you, until it falls.” (Deuteronomy 20:20) So the use is siege works.

Camps aren't in the verse. Moses says to use the trees without fruit “to build siege works against the city that is waging war against you, until it falls.” (Deuteronomy 20:20) That's the job for them.
